title: Chamo-me, levanto-me — pronouns attached to the end of the verb
goal: Take apart the hyphen you've been copying since unit 1. This is the most typically European Portuguese chapter in the whole module: pronoun placement here differs from Brazil, and from every language you may have studied before.
bekal: attaching *me*, *te*, *o*, *a*, *lhe* to the end of the verb
recognizing the six kinds of words that **pull** the pronoun to the front
using reflexive verbs like *levantar-se* and *esquecer-se de*

dialogs.title: Diálogo — As manhãs de cada um
dialogs.intro: Ana and Budi chat about their mornings. It turns out they're both forgetful.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: A que horas é que te levantas?
lines.id: What time do you get up?
lines.literal: at what hours is it that yourself you-raise?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I get up at seven. And you?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Levanto-me tarde, mas também me deito tarde.
lines.id: I get up late, but I also go to bed late.
lines.literal: I-raise-myself late, but also myself I-lay late.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Do you get dressed quickly in the morning?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Não! Demoro imenso. E nunca me lembro das chaves.
lines.id: No! I take ages. And I never remember my keys.
lines.literal: no! I-take-time immensely. and never myself I-remember of-the(pl) keys.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: A mim acontece-me o mesmo. Esqueço-me sempre do telemóvel.
lines.id: Same with me. I always forget my phone.
lines.literal: to me happens-to-me the same. I-forget-myself always of-the phone.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.id: I'll call you in the morning, then!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Boa ideia. Mas não me telefones antes das sete!
lines.id: Good idea. But don't call me before seven!
lines.literal: good idea. but not me you-phone before of-the(pl) seven!

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Combinado. E ao domingo? Também te levantas cedo?
lines.id: Deal. And on Sundays? Do you get up early too?
lines.literal: agreed. and on-the Sunday? also yourself you-raise early?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ao domingo ninguém me acorda. Durmo até ao meio-dia.
lines.id: On Sundays nobody wakes me up. I sleep until noon.
lines.literal: on-the Sunday nobody me wakes. I-sleep until to-the mid-day.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Que sorte! Eu tenho um gato que me acorda às seis.
lines.id: Lucky you! I have a cat that wakes me up at six.
lines.literal: what luck! I I-have a cat that me wakes at-the(pl) six.

notes: **Levanto-me, but também me deito.** Two sentences, one reflexive verb, two different positions — and that is this whole unit in a nutshell. By default, the pronoun sits **after** the verb, joined by a hyphen. But as soon as certain words come before it, it **jumps to the front**.
**Nunca me lembro, not nunca lembro-me.** *Nunca* is one of those pullers. So are *não*, *também*, *já*, *só*, *sempre*, and all question words. The full list is in the table below.
**Ninguém me acorda** — *ninguém* (nobody) also pulls the pronoun forward, because it carries a negation. All negative words do this: *nada*, *ninguém*, *nunca*, *nenhum*.
**Telemóvel is a mobile phone in Portugal**; in Brazil people say *celular*. The word is built from *telefone* + *móvel* and isn't used outside Portugal.
**Combinado** means "agreed" or "OK, deal" — one word that seals a small arrangement. The verb is *combinar*: *Combinamos às oito?* = "Shall we say eight?"
**Coitada de ti** uses *ti* because the preposition *de* comes before it, exactly the rule from unit 11. Note too that *coitada* is feminine, because the person being pitied is Ana.

grammars.title: Object pronouns
body: There are two sets: one for direct objects ("I see **him**") and one for indirect objects ("I say **to him**"). Luckily they only differ in the third person.
after: **At A1 level, the three you really need are *me*, *te* and *lhe*.** All three appear in the most everyday sentences: *ajuda-me*, *vejo-te*, *digo-lhe*.

If the verb ends in *-r*, *-s* or *-z*, that letter **drops** and the pronoun becomes *-lo*, *-la*: *ver + o* → *vê-**lo***, *fazer + a* → *fazê-**la***. Beginners often sidestep this by repeating the noun instead — and that's perfectly fine.

grammars.title: Before or after? Six pullers
body: The default is **after**, with a hyphen. But the six kinds of words below pull it to the front, without a hyphen.

head: The puller
Example
rows: **certain adverbs**: *já, ainda, sempre, também, só, talvez*

after: A practical tip: **if your sentence starts straight with the verb, the pronoun goes after it.** If anything comes before the verb — especially *não* — the pronoun most likely moves to the front too.

**In Brazil, the pronoun almost always goes in front**, even at the start of a sentence: *me chamo Budi*, *te vejo amanhã*. In Portugal that order sounds wrong, and in formal writing it is considered wrong. If you've learned from Brazilian songs or soap operas, this is the habit you'll need to reverse.

grammars.title: Reflexive verbs
body: A group of verbs always comes with a pronoun pointing back at the subject. The dictionary form is written with *-se* at the end.

head: Infinitive
Meaning
*eu*
*tu*
rows: to lie down, go to bed

after: Notice that the pronoun changes with the subject: *me* for *eu*, *te* for *tu*, *se* for *ele/ela/você*, *nos* for *nós*, *se* for *eles*.
The last two require *de*: *lembro-me **da** Ana*, *esqueci-me **das** chaves*. Just like *gostar de*, the preposition can't be dropped.
*Vestir-se* and *sentir-se* change their vowel in the *eu* form: **visto-me**, **sinto-me** — the same group as *dormir* and *preferir*.

sections.title: A day from waking up to bedtime

head: Português
Say it
English
rows: to go to bed, lie down

blocks.text: **Acordar and levantar-se are not the same thing**, and Portuguese makes you choose. *Acordo às seis, mas só me levanto às sete* = "I wake up at six, but I don't get up until seven". English draws the same line between "wake up" and "get up".

blocks.title: Everyday phrases with attached pronouns
items: *Vejo-te amanhã!* — "See you tomorrow!" One of the most common goodbyes.
*Diz-me uma coisa...* — "Tell me something...", a very Portuguese way to open a question.
*Desculpa, não te ouvi.* — "Sorry, I didn't hear you." Note how *não* pulls *te* to the front.
*Chamo-me...* — which you've used since unit 1, and now you know why it looks like that.
